data.title: Structural biology of microbial enzymes.
data.description: Structural biology of microbial enzymes Our knowledge of microbial biology is expanding, greatly assisted by the availability of genomic data. This contributes an improved understanding of how existing antimicrobial drugs work and which metabolic pathways and component enzymes represent potential new drug targets. That is, which enzymes are essential for the survival of parasites or bacteria, which are absent in the human host or present markedly differing substrate specificity. An enzyme can be validated as a target, genetically or chemically although in the latter case with a reliance on already having a potent inhibitor, and then exploited by a structure-based approach to the development of new therapies. Such research is important given the urgent requirement for new treatments to combat protozoan and bacterial infection. The front-line drugs for trypanosomatid infections have never been good with serious and undesirable side effects and now drug resistant parasites are increasingly prevalent. Drug resistant bacteria are also a serious concern and new drugs are sough, especially for organisms such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A multidisciplinary basic research programme has been designed to improve understanding of enzyme-ligand interactions and to delineate mechanism in three areas. (I) Oxidative stress and redox regulation in protozoan parasites, (II) Pterin/folate metabolism of trypanosomatids and (III) Isoprenoid biosynthesis in pathogenic bacteria and apicomplexans. It is my ambition to utilise the results and contribute to the development of improved treatments for a range of infections, in particular parasitic diseases.

data.title: Leukocyte recruitment and effector mechanisms in intestinal helminth infection.
data.description: The global prevalence of gastrointestinal nematodes is overwhelming. Causing morbidity rather than mortality, these parasites alter and compromise immunity to other types of infection and the ability to successfully vaccinate. Knowledge of the cell regulatory mechanisms which underlie resistance (Th2) or susceptibility (Th1) to infection is comprehensive, yet knowledge of how protective immunity is mediated remains fragmented. Emerging from my current programme of work is a key role for Th2 controlled innate effectors and innate effector cells, which precipitate worm expulsion whilst preventing immunopathology. These discoveries have advanced my programme significantly and are now the urgent areas to investigate. Colonic macrophages dominate the cellular infiltration post Trichuris muris infection yet their functional role is unknown. We will explore the phenotype and function of colonic macrophages in resistant and susceptible mice to identify effector or regulatory roles. Also dominating in gut tissue of resistant mice are transcripts for members of the angiogenin family. We will explore the biology of the angiogenins, including roles as novel anti-parasite innate effector molecules. Our key goals are: To phenotype and functionally analyse the colonic macrophage in mice resistant and susceptible to Trichuris muris. To explore the biology of the angiogenins and their anti-parasitic effects.

data.title: The role of growth factor signalling in mesoderm formation and morphogenesis in Xenopus.
data.description: Embryogenesis in vertebrate organisms results from a succession of inductive processes. In frogs the first induction occurs prior to gastrulation when signals emanating from the vegetal hemisphere cause the formation of mesoderm in the equatorial region of the embryo. The second event occurs during gastrulation when the dorsal mesoderm, termed the organiser, patterns the mesoderm and induces the neural ectoderm. As a long term goal I would like to understand that molecular basis of the inductions that organise the vertebrate embryo. In addition I would like to better understand how localised production of signalling molecules gets translated into organised changes in cell movement and differentiation, resulting in normal embryogenesis. As a first step toward understanding the molecular mechanism of vertebrate pattern formation I have been investigating the role of growth factor signalling during mesoderm induction. Evidence obtained in the past seven years suggests that peptide growth factors are involved in this inductive process. For example, fibroblast growth factor (FGF) and activin have been shown to induce mesoderm in isolated explants. To demonstrate an endogenous function for FGF signalling during mesoderm induction, I constructed a dominant negative mutation of the FGF receptor. Using this, I have shown that FGF signalling is required for the induction of most of the mesoderm in the early embryo. In addition I have shown that dorsal mesoderm in embryos expressing the dominant negative FGF receptor fails to produce the signals necessary for the patterning of the embryo at the gastrula stage. In this proposal I intend to exploit this observation in order to gain a better understanding of the mechanism of pattern formation in the frog embryo. First I propose to fully characterise the types of inductions missing in dorsal mesoderm expressing the dominant negative FGF receptor. Then I will investigate whether the deficient inductions can be supplied by known putative signalling molecules. I also propose a functional assay that may lead to the isolation putative signalling molecules of the dorsal mesoderm. In addition I propose a scheme for isolating genes that require FGF signalling for their expression. Finally I propose experiments that address the question of how morphogen gradients result in patterning of tissues.

data.title: Mechanisms of natural tolerance and the role of the musocal immune system.
data.description: Mucosal immune responses are actively regulated to prevent development of harmful cell mediated immune responses, yet little is known about the cell types and cytokines involved in this regulation. Two broad approaches will be used to identify the basic mechanisms of mucosal immune regulation. In the first, a recently described murine model of colitis with similarities to Crohn's disease in man, which develops spontaneously in SCID mice restored with CD45RBhigh CD4+ T cells from normal donors and is completely prevented by co-transfer of the reciprocal CD45RBlow population, will be used to investigate mechanisms of disease induction and prevention. The mechanism of action of the regulatory CD45RBlow population will be dissected in vivo, including identification of immunosuppressive cytokines and their cellular source, which are critical for suppression of disease and effects of the CD45RBlow population on the homing properties of CD45RBhigh population. Experiments using gnotobiotic mice suggest components of the normal flora are involved in disease induction and these experiments will be extended to identify the antigen specificity of cells which cause disease and those that prevent it. The second approach will involve study of T-helper cell subset differentiation in the gastrointestinal tract in both tolerance and non- responsiveness. A TCR transgenic mouse line will be used to determine which T helper cell subsets are induced by oral tolerance regimes compared with oral immunisation and which cytokines are involved in the differentiation and effector functions of these cells. Recent evidence suggests that induction of TGF-ß and IL-10 producing regulatory cells may be an important component of oral tolerance. A genetic approach will be taken to allow the detection of IL-10 producing cells in vivo, providing information on the anatomical location of regulatory cells within the gut associated lymphoid tissue. The results of these experiments should define the rules that govern T helper cell subset differentiation in the gut, providing a basis for manipulation of T helper cell responses to ingested antigen. This may be particularly useful in a number of autoimmune diseases where induction of cells that suppress cell mediated immune responses is desirable.

data.title: Intestinal homeostasis: identification of the factors that influence the balance between regulatory and effector cells in the intestine and how alterations in these can lead to chronic intestinal inflammation.
data.description: Using mouse models we have shown that colitis can develop as a consequence of excessive innate or T cell dependent responses and that these can be controlled by immune suppressive regulatory T cells (TR). Our recent studies suggest compartmentalization of the pathological response with IL-23 driving local intestinal inflammation and IL-12 mediating the systemic response. We will further characterize the cellular and molecular pathways of IL-23 driven intestinal inflammation, including IL-17 production, to identify their role in innate and T cell dependent colitis. Foxp3 and IL-10 indicator mice will be used to analyse the distribution of bacteria-induced and naturally arising TR cells in vivo as they respond to inflammation and determine their functional properties in distinct anatomical compartments. CD103+ mucosal DC's plays a key role in TR function and will determine how this DC subset influences the balance between effector and TR responses. We have also newly identified the G-protein coupled receptor Gpr 83 as a potential marker for TR cells and using Gpr83-/- mice we will assess its functional role. The results of these studies will facilitate the development of novel therapeutics for chronic inflammatory diseases via the manipulation of TR cells and tissue specific inflammatory pathways.

data.title: Eating disorders and obesity: cognitive processes and treatments.
data.description: The research has three aims. The first is to identify the factors and processes involved in the aetiology and maintenance of eating disorders. The second is to use this information to develop improved methods for their treatment. The third is to extend this work to the maintenance and treatment of obesity. The programme involves five complementary epidemiological and treatment studies. The aim of the first study is to identify those factors which combine with dieting to distinguish dieters who develop bulimia nervosa from those who do not. The second study is designed to identify risk factors for the development of bulimia nervosa and a variant termed "binge eating disorder". The third study investigates the relative and combined influence of cognitive and interpersonal mechanisms on the course of eating disorders. The fourth study complements the third by investigating the action of cognitive and interpersonal treatments, thereby further illuminating the role of cognitive and interpersonal maintaining mechanisms. The fifth study is on obesity. It involves the evaluation of a new cognitive treatment and the cognitive account of weight regain upon which it is based.

data.title: Implications of bacterial evolution and population structure for public health: the Neisseria model.
data.description: Many pathogens of man are antigenically variable, using changes in the structure of cell components that are exposed to the immune system as a means of evading immune attack. This strategy poses substantial difficulties for the development of public health interventions, particularly vaccination. In addition, the evolution of antigenic variants and the accommodation of such variants within the structural constraints of the cell surface are important fundamental phenomena. The existence of pathogenic species as 'strains' that are antigenically distinct has been known for most of this century but the evolution of 'pathogenic' strains and the reasons for their stability in the face of recombination and diversifying selection remain poorly understood. This project will improve our understanding of the evolution of antigenic variants by the acquisition and analysis of data from populations of the human pathogen Neisseria meningitidis specifically to apply, test, and develop models of the evolution of antigenic variation. The range and rate of antigenic variation in each sub-population of meningococci will be established and the following specific hypotheses will be addressed: (i) that meningococci have a range of population structures that are associated with specific epidemiologies; (ii) that the antigenic diversity of distinct meningococcal sub-populations differ in both level of diversity and in the mutational mechanisms most important in generating that diversity; (iii) that meningococcal populations are structured into strains by human immune interactions, and that any differences observed in (i) and (ii) are the result of differing selection pressures in diverse epidemiological contexts; (iv) that nucleotide sequence data can be used to predict antigens that are likely to be of use in vaccine design. These data will be used to validate and develop further models of antigenic variation and its effect on clonal divergence and epidemiology.

data.title: COP I vesicle coat proteins in membrane traffic: structure/function analysis using mutants and domain-specific interactions with regulators and cargo.
data.Sponsor(s): Prof George Dickson, Prof John Paul Luzio
data.description: The functions, regulation and membrane targeting of non-clathrin coat proteins (COPs) will be studied using the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a genetically tractable model organism. These cytoplasmic proteins form an electron-dense membrane coat around transport vesicles which are essential for transfer of proteins among early compartments of the secretory pathway in all eukaryotic cells. COPs are required for the retrieval of KKXX-tagged type I membrane proteins, and probably other proteins, from the Golgi complex to the ER, and probably also for forward ER-to-Golgi traffic; however, their exact role in eukaryotic membrane traffic is currently controversial. The longer term goal of the proposed research is to understand at a molecular level how non-clathrin coated vesicles form and how COPs mediate the sorting of intended cargo proteins. Due to my previous work, and the work of others, all seven subunits of the cytoplasmic assembly unit of the non-clathrin coat, termed coatomer, have now been cloned and sequenced and mutants are available. I will study the structure of the coatomer complex, the spatial arrangements of its subunits, and interactions with proteins on vesicle membranes using genetic and biochemical techniques. Specifically, I will study interactions of coatomer and coatomer subcomplexes with KKXX-tagged proteins and other classes of vesicle cargo proteins, as well as with the small GTPase ARF and potential membrane receptors in in vitro binding assays. I will use systematic truncation analysis of COPs expressed in yeast or bacteria to analyse the essential functions of individual COPs and map domains responsible for molecular interactions with proteins within and outside the coatomer complex. I expect as yet unidentified membrane proteins to be involved in the selection of vesicle budding sites; other proteins are likely involved in the release of KKXX-binding and regulation of the coat assembly/disassembly cycle. My goal is to identify such novel gene products, especially membrane-associated proteins that regulate coat function, genetically. I propose several different genetic approaches for their identification. Subsequently these novel genes will be disrupted, conditional alleles will be constructed and antibodies will be raised against them. I will study the functions of these novel proteins further using yeast genetics in combination with biochemistry and cell biological techniques. I will also test genetically and biochemically whether coatomer can interact with other sequence motifs that carry protein sorting information for intracellular trafficking, e.g. a novel RR-motif present on type II membrane proteins.

data.title: Investigation of the signalling and physiological role played by agonist- mediated phosphorylation of Gq/11-coupled receptors.
data.description: Studies on the Mechanisms and Functional Consequences of Phospholipase C-Coupled Receptor Phosphorylation Many neurotransmitter, neuromodulator, hormone and growth factor receptors are coupled, via G-proteins, to the activation of phospholipase C (PLC). The processes that regulate this signal transduction pathway are, therefore, central in the cellular responses mediated by a diverse group of biological ligands, in addition to being important for the action of many therapeutic drugs. This project proposes to investigate the involvement of receptor phosphorylation in the regulation of PLC-coupled receptors. The investigation is aimed at three levels; (i) identification of the kinases responsible for PLC-coupled receptor phosphorylation, (ii) the functional consequences of receptor phosphorylation and (iii) the relevance of phosphorylation to signalling in an intact tissue; airway smooth muscle. I have recently been successful in the purification of a novel receptor-specific kinase (MRK) that is able to phosphorylate the PLC- coupled m3-muscarinic receptor. One of the major aims of this project is to obtain a cDNA clone for MRK. Analysis of the modes of MRK regulation will also be conducted, in addition, to investigation of the receptor-substrate specificity of MRK. Functional studies on the role receptor phosphorylation plays in the regulation of receptor/PLC coupling will form an important part of the project. This will benefit from the excellent infra-structure already in place in the department, that allows for a mix of molecular approaches and detailed analysis of receptor-signalling properties. It is planned to identify the sites of phosphorylation on the PLC-coupled m1- and m3-muscarinic receptors and delete these sites by point mutagenesis. Detailed functional analysis of mutant and wild type receptors will then be pursued. This will be coupled with reconstitution studies, and transfection studies where muscarinic receptor subtypes will be co-expressed with receptor-specific kinases and dominant negative kinase mutants. Particular emphasis will be placed on the possible role phosphorylation plays in receptor desensitisation, and receptor/G-protein coupling.

data.title: Functions of sialic acid binding lectins (siglecs) in the innate immune system.
data.description: The Sialoadhesin family is a recently-characterised subgroup of the immunoglobulin superfamily comprising sialoadhesin, CD22, the myelin associated glycoprotein (MAG) and CD33. These proteins mediate cell-cell interactions via recognition of distinct sialylated glycoconjugates and are involved in diverse functions, ranging from myelopoiesis (sialoadhesin and CD33) and activation of B cells (CD22) to regulation of neuronal growth (MAG). I propose to study the structure, properties and biological functions of these proteins, with particular emphasis on sialoadhesin and CD33. Sialoadhesin is expressed by stromal macrophages and interacts with developing myeloid cells in the bone marrow where it is implicated in their growth and survival. CD33 is a myeloid antigen first expressed on early progenitor cells, suggesting a role in myeloid cell differentiation. I propose the following: 1. A detailed structure-function analysis will be carried out on the V-set domain of sialoadhesin, previously shown to contain the sialic acid binding site, in order to understand the molecular basis for recognition of distinct types of sialic acids and their glycosidic linkages. 2. Endogenous ligands recognised by sialoadhesin and CD33 will be isolated and the structure of their oligosaccharides will be determined. Polypeptide carriers will be sequenced and molecularly cloned where appropriate. 3. Sialoadhesin has seventeen Ig domains whereas CD33 has two. As recombinant proteins they exhibit similar binding properties but when expressed in plasma membranes only sialoadhesin can bind cells. We will test our 'rain forest model' for the evolution of sialoadhesin by generating a panel of CHO cell lines expressing deletion mutants and determining the minimal number of domains required to mediate binding. The effect of cross-linking sialoadhesin ligands on the survival of myeloid cells will also be studied. Inhibitory antibodies will be injected into mice to examine functional changes in haemopoiesis. The function of sialoadhesin will also be investigated using transgenic mice either lacking sialoadhesin or expressing it ectopically under the control of the CD11b promoter.

data.title: Mechanisms of social interaction.
data.description: While I am already supported by the Wellcome Trust, my position is currently as a component of the grant awarded to Richard Frackowiak. On the basis of past career and current work it is more appropriate for me to have independent funding. The work I plan will generate a substantial series of linked experiments in a number of cognitive domains. I anticipate that much of the day to day work will be carried out by a series of research fellows and PhD students. Long-term funding for the coordinator of this group is essential to provide continuity and coherence across these projects and to ensure an optimum environment for the training of a new generation of clinical neuroscientists. In addition, a long-term view is needed to ensure that the work of my group continues to feed into and benefit from developments in the other groups that compose the Functional Imaging Laboratory. Functional imaging techniques, particularly fMRI, are going to change and develop rapidly over the next ten years. My past career demonstrates that I have the flexibility to learn and take advantage of new developments as they arise. Long-term funding will obviate the shot-term risks associated with the exploitation of these new developments. My fundamental aim is to increase understanding of brain abnormalities underlying psychosis. Of necessity this is a long-term goal since much work on normal brain function is needed before cognitive paradigms and brain imaging techniques can be applied to the study of psychosis. This work will span at least a ten year period.

data.title: Protein crystallography: development of new methods and application to the study of pathogenesis.
data.description: I propose to conduct research in two areas of protein crystallography: the determination of crystal structures of medically-relevant proteins, and the development of theory and methods. The general focus of my group is on structures of potential drug or vaccine targets, which aid the development of new therapies. The proteins we are studying include several bacterial virulence factors. Structural studies of pertussis toxin are building a basis for the design of whooping cough vaccines. The structures of cell-binding B-subunits of E. coli Shiga-like toxin are allowing the cyclical design of improved ligands, which can be used as drugs to adsorb the toxin in the gut before it acts. The mechanism by which enteropathogenic E. coli adhere to the intestinal epithelium will be studied by determining the structure of EaeB. Other structural studies involve the serpin family of serine proteinase inhibitors and related proteins. A major goal is to clarify serpin mechanism by determining the structure of a complex with a proteinase. As well, the structure of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 will be determined in its active state, followed by complexes with potential thrombolytic drugs. I have also begun to initiate new collaborations with other proposed members of the Institute. In crystallographic theory, I will continue to work on structure factor probability distributions, which have led to improved electron density maps and more powerful structure refinement. The power of these methods will be increased by generalising the probability distributions, and their application will be extended to the technique of density modification.

data.title: Genetic analysis of susceptibility to depression.
data.description: Mapping the susceptibility loci for psychiatric disorders has so far proved difficult because the intensive interviewing necessary for reliable diagnosis has prohibited the collection of the large sample sizes needed to detect relatively small genetic effects. We propose an alternative strategy: to map neuroticism, a major genetic mediator of at least two common psychiatric disorders, major depression and generalized anxiety disorder. Neuroticism is a quantitative trait that can be scored reliably and easily by the completion of a questionnaire, the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ). It has been shown that in many cases mapping quantitative trait loci (QTLs) is a more powerful approach than mapping qualitative traits, but even so many thousands of sib pairs are needed to detect loci with low heritabilities. Recent statistical analyses have demonstrated that most of the statistical power comes from sampling pairs that are either discordant or concordant thus making it possible to genotype a fraction of the total sample and yet maintain power. We have used existing estimates of the heritability, mode of inheritance and sibling correlations for neuroticism to simulate sampling strategies. These simulations lead us to propose genotyping 900 sib pairs and the parents of half the sample to detect a locus with a heritability of 10% in the most likely situations with a power of over 80%. To reduce the environmental variance of the EPQ measure, we will use a re-screening strategy. On the basis of a pilot study of our recruitment method, we estimate that by contacting 100,000 patients on the lists of 40 Oxfordshire general practices we will be able to recruit 900 sib pairs for this study.

data.title: Molecular basis of leukocyte recognition and activation
data.description: Many of the functions of leukocytes are initiated by protein-protein interactions at the cell surface. An understanding of the structural basis of such interactions is therefore likely to be important in the developing therapeutic strategies based on manipulating the immune system. Crystallographic and nuclear magnetic resonance-based structural studies, allied with mutational, kinetic and thermodynamic analyses, are providing important insights into the structural basis of protein-protein interactions involving the T-cell recognition molecule, CD2, which participates in the cell-recognition, and CD59, which is involved in lateral interactions within the membrane. It is therefore proposed that these studies continue and that the structural work be extended to include studies of the interactions of CD28 and CTLA-4 with their ligands so that the general mechanisms of low-affinity protein-protein recognition at the cell surface can be defined. It is also suggested that many cell surface molecules at the T-cell surface function as part of macromolecular ensembles rather than as individual molecules and, to illustrate this concept, a new model of T cell triggering has been proposed. It is argued that the generation of such models, and the understanding of T-cell biology in general, would be significantly enhanced if it was clear that the majority of genes encoding cell surface molecules had been identified. It is proposed, therefore, that a new method, the serial analysis of gene expression, which allows rapid quantitative and qualitative comparisons of gene expression within and between tissues, be undertaken and used as a basis for the complementary, systematic identification of the complement of genes encoding T-cell specific surface molecules.

data.title: Functional imaging studies of language processing.
data.description: The research program I am proposing will use non-invasive brain imaging, in particular positron emission tomography (PET) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), to identify the functional anatomy of language in normal and language impaired subjects. My8 hypothesis is that functional specialisation within the language system involves both segregation and integration of activity in connected cortical regions. This organisation principal has been well established in visual neuroscience and is providing a very useful framework for studying the language system. My investigations will focus on characterising the nature of semantic and phonological processing and the interaction of these systems with the sensory input and motor output processes service them. The experiments planned will pursue three distinct types of functional segregation : (1) modality specificity, (2) functional specificity, and (3) category specificity. Modality specificity relates to the mode of sensory input (eg visual versus auditory) including the stimulus type within a sensory mode (e.g. visual words versus objects). Functional specificity relates to the functional subcomponents within a system (eg visual knowledge versus functional knowledge or phonological analysis versus phonological retrieval); and category specificity relates to processing differences between categories of object or concept (eg animate versus inanimate or concrete versus abstract). In order to integrate the results from these studies into a coherent model of language processing, a consistent style of experimental design will be adopted in all experiments. This will involve multi-factorial task designs to distinguish functional segregation that is context independent (eg common to all modalities) from functional segregation that is context specific (e.g. specific to one modality). Such an approach should provide a new perspective on our current understanding of language processing and ultimately could facilitate the work of those responsible for prognosis and therapy of language impaired patients.

data.title: Mechansims and actions of cyclic ADP-ribose and NAADP-mediated calcium signalling.
data.description: This proposal will test the hypothesis that a family of pyridine nucleotide metabolites are part of a multifunctional signalling pathway leading to the generation of complex Ca2+ signals within cells. Intracellular Ca2+ ions are universal regulators of physiological and pathological processes. Intracellular Ca2+ signals are often organised as repetitive spikes and as propagating regenerative waves. These complex signals may arise from the coordinated activation of both plasma membrane and intracellular Ca2+ channels. Of the two classes of intracellular channels, the physiological control of inositol trisphosphat (IP3) receptors by IP3 which in turn is generated by well understood signal transduction pathways, is clearly documented. In contrast, the signalling molecules and transduction pathways leading to modulation of ryanodine receptors (RyRs), the other channel class, are poorly characterized. One obvious candidate as a RyR regulator is the endogenous molecule, cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR). It has been proposed that Ca2+ mobilization from internal stores I under dual control by both IP3 and cADPR as intracellular messengers. cADPR has been implicated in the regulation of biomedically important events such as cardiac contractility, insulin secretion, neuromodulation and fertilization. Two roles for cADPR in Ca2+ signalling have been proposed. The first is as classical second messenger, whose levels are regulated by extracellular stimuli, while a second role as a modulator of the Ca2+ sensitivity of Ca2+ release channels has also been advanced. We will establish unequivocally the physiological role of cADPR as an intracellular messenger/regulator of the 'excitability' of Ca2+ release mechanisms controlling the production of Ca2+ signals within and between cells. Great importance will be attached to the identification of mechanisms that control the cellular levels of cADPR. The research will use a multidisciplinary approach to discover the mechanisms and roles of these molecules in cellular regulation and the elucidation of the signal transduction pathways controlling their levels, perhaps offering novel targets for therapeutic intervention.

data.title: Molecular mechanisms mediating immune evasion in African trypanosomes.
data.description: We would like to unravel the various mechanisms mediating antigenic variation in the African trypanosome Trypanosoma brucei. Recently techniques have been developed to transfect infective bloodstream form trypanosomes, which is now allowing us to modify the active VSG expression site and test the subsequent effect on switching. We would like to concentrate primarily on VSG expression site control. VSG expression sites are invariably located on chromosome ends, or telomeres. First we would like to test the hypothesis that they are controlled by a mechanism analogous to Telomere Position Effect in yeast. If so, trypanosomes would be the first organism found to use an analogous phenomenon to control the expression of multiple functional transcription units. We would like to disrupt the repressed chromatin state present in VSG expression sites in one of three ways: 1) We would like to generate trypanosomes which overexpress N-terminal deletions of histone H4. These truncated histones should be incapable of recruiting the SIR proteins necessary to establish the repressed state. 2) We would like to clone and knock-out one of the most conserved of the repressing SIR proteins (SIR 2) which should result in trypanosomes with (partially) derepressed VSG expression sites. 3) Chemicals are available which interfere with histone deacetylation, which results in transcription derepression in other organisms. We would like to see if any of these work in, or are specific for trypanosomes. As we have reason to believe that VSG expression derepression will be lethal, any effective agent with specificity for the parasite is a possible trypanocidal drug. The rigorously mutually exclusive nature of bloodstream VSG expression site transcription is a mystery. We have trypanosomes with drug resistance genes inserted into an active and an inactive VSG expression site. Selection for double expression results in very poor growth. We would like to find out why. In addition, we would like to know more about the size of the repressed domain encompassing the silent VSG expression sites. We would like to establish how the parasites can live with powerful effects operating at the telomeres which don't disrupt critical housekeeping genes. Lastly, we would like to know more about the frequencies with which different switching events, including those mediated by gene conversions, occur during an infection. Hopefully this will allow us to design more sophisticated models for VSG switching which include more recent biochemical insights into how trypanosomes switch their coat.
